This loss of control is strictly limited to food and eating. I manage every other part of my life very carefully and meticulously, so I've never experienced anything like this in a sexual context or any other area.\n\nDoctor: How often do these episodes of uncontrollable eating occur, and have you noticed any pattern or trigger that seems to lead up to them?\n\nPatient: These episodes have been happening about once a week for the past five months. They usually trigger in the evenings when I'm alone after my wife goes to sleep or when I'm staying up doing paperwork, especially since my doctor warned me about my blood pressure and weight.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe if there's any sexual behavior or fantasies that you feel are excessive or difficult to control, even if you mentioned it's not similar to the eating episodes, to help clarify some diagnostic possibilities?\n\nPatient: No, I don't experience anything like that. I don't have any excessive or uncontrollable sexual behaviors or fantasies, as that is just not something I struggle with. My difficulties are strictly around my eating.\n\nDoctor: Do you often eat very rapidly during these episodes or eat until you feel uncomfortably full, and have you noticed if these episodes are preceded by a feeling of tension that is relieved by eating?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure about eating particularly fast or feeling a release of tension. For me, it feels more like I'm just on autopilot, consuming a large amount of food because I'm feeling lonely in the evenings or worried about my health.\n\nDoctor: During these episodes of eating, do you experience a sense of guilt or self-criticism specifically about the act of eating itself, or is it more about the fear of gaining weight or health consequences?\n\nPatient: It’s really a mix of both, as I feel deeply frustrated with myself right after for losing control of my eating. But a massive driver of my anxiety is the panic about the scale creeping up and my blood pressure getting worse, which is why I end up forcing myself to throw up to get the bad stuff out before it turns into extra weight.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me more about when you started forcing yourself to throw up after eating, and how often this behavior occurs in relation to your episodes of uncontrollable eating?\n\nPatient: I started forcing myself to throw up about five months ago, right when these out-of-control eating episodes first began after my doctor's checkup. It happens about once a week, specifically on the nights when I overeat, because I feel desperate to get the bad stuff out of my system before it turns into extra weight.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate how often you engage in self-induced vomiting as a means to compensate for the calories consumed during these episodes, and does this behavior occur exclusively after the uncontrollable eating episodes or at other times as well?\n\nPatient: I make myself throw up about once a week, and it only ever happens right after those nights when I lose control and overeat. I never do it at any other time during the week. It is strictly a desperate attempt to get the food out of my system so it doesn't turn into extra weight.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever used any other methods to compensate for the calories consumed, such as excessive exercise, laxatives, or diuretics, in addition to self-induced vomiting?\n\nPatient: No, I’ve never used laxatives, water pills, or done any kind of extreme workouts. Honestly, besides making myself throw up to get the bad stuff out, the only other thing I do is try to rigidly restrict my eating the next day to make up for it.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any physical symptoms or health concerns as a result of your self-induced vomiting, such as tooth problems, throat issues, or electrolyte imbalances?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't noticed any of those specific issues like tooth or throat problems. However, I do often feel quite worn out and queasy the next morning.\n\nDoctor: Besides self-induced vomiting, do you also use other purging methods like laxatives, diuretics, or enemas to compensate for the calories consumed during these episodes?\n\nPatient: No, I have never used laxatives, diuretics, or enemas. Forcing myself to throw up is the only method I use to get the bad food out of my system.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate the average amount of weight you try to maintain or lose through these behaviors of binge eating followed by self-induced vomiting and dietary restriction?\n\nPatient: I don't really have a specific target weight or a set number of pounds I'm trying to lose. It's more about a general fear of gaining any weight at all and wanting to prevent the scale from going up. I just panic at the thought of putting on even a pound or two.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm if your self-induced vomiting and dietary restriction behaviors are primarily aimed at preventing weight gain, rather than addressing any body image concerns or a perceived need to be extremely thin?\n\nPatient: It's actually a combination of both, because while I desperately want to prevent weight gain so I don't slide into getting \"old and fat,\" I also struggle deeply with my body image. I catch myself feeling like my entire worth as a husband and professional is tied to whether my gut is hanging over my belt. I don't need to be extremely thin, but I'm terrified of looking out of shape and letting myself go.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your fear of gaining weight and your concerns about body image influence your decision to engage in binge eating followed by purging, and do you feel that these behaviors are necessary to maintain a sense of self-worth or control over your appearance?"
  }

Reply naturally in English as the Patient to the last Doctor utterance.\nAnswer only the question, in 2–3 sentences maximum.\n\n[Dialogue]\nDoctor: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see us today?\n\nPatient: Thank you for seeing me, doctor. To be honest, once I start eating in the evenings, it feels like I can’t stop myself, no matter how much I tell myself I should. It has really started to frighten me because I'm usually a very disciplined person.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe a typical episode where you feel like you can't stop eating, and do you experience any feelings of guilt or shame afterwards?\n\nPatient: Typically, after my wife goes to bed, I’ll start with some leftovers but end up eating half a pan of macaroni and cheese, fried chicken, and snacks like my hands are on autopilot. Afterward, I feel this deep sense of regret and shame because I just couldn't stop myself. It really frightens me how completely out of control I feel in those moments.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced similar episodes of feeling out of control, but in a sexual context, or is this loss of control primarily related to eating?\n\nPatient: No, nothing like that at all. This loss of control is strictly limited to food and eating. I manage every other part of my life very carefully and meticulously, so I've never experienced anything like this in a sexual context or any other area.\n\nDoctor: How often do these episodes of uncontrollable eating occur, and have you noticed any pattern or trigger that seems to lead up to them?\n\nPatient: These episodes have been happening about once a week for the past five months. They usually trigger in the evenings when I'm alone after my wife goes to sleep or when I'm staying up doing paperwork, especially since my doctor warned me about my blood pressure and weight.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe if there's any sexual behavior or fantasies that you feel are excessive or difficult to control, even if you mentioned it's not similar to the eating episodes, to help clarify some diagnostic possibilities?\n\nPatient: No, I don't experience anything like that. I don't have any excessive or uncontrollable sexual behaviors or fantasies, as that is just not something I struggle with. My difficulties are strictly around my eating.\n\nDoctor: Do you often eat very rapidly during these episodes or eat until you feel uncomfortably full, and have you noticed if these episodes are preceded by a feeling of tension that is relieved by eating?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure about eating particularly fast or feeling a release of tension. For me, it feels more like I'm just on autopilot, consuming a large amount of food because I'm feeling lonely in the evenings or worried about my health.\n\nDoctor: During these episodes of eating, do you experience a sense of guilt or self-criticism specifically about the act of eating itself, or is it more about the fear of gaining weight or health consequences?\n\nPatient: It’s really a mix of both, as I feel deeply frustrated with myself right after for losing control of my eating. But a massive driver of my anxiety is the panic about the scale creeping up and my blood pressure getting worse, which is why I end up forcing myself to throw up to get the bad stuff out before it turns into extra weight.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me more about when you started forcing yourself to throw up after eating, and how often this behavior occurs in relation to your episodes of uncontrollable eating?\n\nPatient: I started forcing myself to throw up about five months ago, right when these out-of-control eating episodes first began after my doctor's checkup. It happens about once a week, specifically on the nights when I overeat, because I feel desperate to get the bad stuff out of my system before it turns into extra weight.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate how often you engage in self-induced vomiting as a means to compensate for the calories consumed during these episodes, and does this behavior occur exclusively after the uncontrollable eating episodes or at other times as well?\n\nPatient: I make myself throw up about once a week, and it only ever happens right after those nights when I lose control and overeat. I never do it at any other time during the week. It is strictly a desperate attempt to get the food out of my system so it doesn't turn into extra weight.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever used any other methods to compensate for the calories consumed, such as excessive exercise, laxatives, or diuretics, in addition to self-induced vomiting?\n\nPatient: No, I’ve never used laxatives, water pills, or done any kind of extreme workouts. Honestly, besides making myself throw up to get the bad stuff out, the only other thing I do is try to rigidly restrict my eating the next day to make up for it.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any physical symptoms or health concerns as a result of your self-induced vomiting, such as tooth problems, throat issues, or electrolyte imbalances?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't noticed any of those specific issues like tooth or throat problems. However, I do often feel quite worn out and queasy the next morning.\n\nDoctor: Besides self-induced vomiting, do you also use other purging methods like laxatives, diuretics, or enemas to compensate for the calories consumed during these episodes?\n\nPatient: No, I have never used laxatives, diuretics, or enemas. Forcing myself to throw up is the only method I use to get the bad food out of my system.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate the average amount of weight you try to maintain or lose through these behaviors of binge eating followed by self-induced vomiting and dietary restriction?\n\nPatient: I don't really have a specific target weight or a set number of pounds I'm trying to lose. It's more about a general fear of gaining any weight at all and wanting to prevent the scale from going up. I just panic at the thought of putting on even a pound or two.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm if your self-induced vomiting and dietary restriction behaviors are primarily aimed at preventing weight gain, rather than addressing any body image concerns or a perceived need to be extremely thin?\n\nPatient: It's actually a combination of both, because while I desperately want to prevent weight gain so I don't slide into getting \"old and fat,\" I also struggle deeply with my body image. I catch myself feeling like my entire worth as a husband and professional is tied to whether my gut is hanging over my belt. I don't need to be extremely thin, but I'm terrified of looking out of shape and letting myself go.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your fear of gaining weight and your concerns about body image influence your decision to engage in binge eating followed by purging, and do you feel that these behaviors are necessary to maintain a sense of self-worth or control over your appearance?\n\nPatient: Yes, they absolutely drive the purging, because when I think about gaining even a single pound, I panic and feel like my entire worth as a husband and professional is reduced to how my gut looks in a dress shirt. Forcing myself to throw up feels like a desperate, necessary way to \"get the bad stuff out\" before it can turn into extra weight. It's the only way I feel like I can regain a little bit of control after completely losing it during the binge.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if your binge eating episodes are typically followed by purging through self-induced vomiting as a way to compensate for the consumed calories, and does this behavior occur frequently enough to be considered a regular pattern?\n\nPatient: Yes, it has definitely become a regular pattern over the last five months. On the nights when I overeat, I always end up in the bathroom forcing myself to throw up to \"get the bad stuff out\" so it doesn't turn into extra weight. This happens pretty much once a week, right after those episodes.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm if your episodes of binge eating followed by self-induced vomiting occur regularly, such as once a week, and if this pattern has been consistent over the past five months?\n\nPatient: Yes, that is exactly correct. For about the past five months, there has been at least one night every week where I have eaten an unusually large amount of food and then forced myself to throw up afterward to try to undo it. It has been a very consistent, weekly pattern for me.\n\nDoctor: Do you experience a significant amount of fear or anxiety about gaining weight, even when you're at a normal weight, which drives your need to purge after binge eating?"

It feels like the only way to prevent the food from sitting on me as extra weight the next day.

They usually trigger in the evenings when I'm alone after my wife goes to sleep or when I'm staying up doing paperwork, especially since my doctor warned me about my blood pressure and weight.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe if there's any sexual behavior or fantasies that you feel are excessive or difficult to control, even if you mentioned it's not similar to the eating episodes, to help clarify some diagnostic possibilities?\n\nPatient: No, I don't experience anything like that. I don't have any excessive or uncontrollable sexual behaviors or fantasies, as that is just not something I struggle with. My difficulties are strictly around my eating.\n\nDoctor: Do you often eat very rapidly during these episodes or eat until you feel uncomfortably full, and have you noticed if these episodes are preceded by a feeling of tension that is relieved by eating?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure about eating particularly fast or feeling a release of tension. For me, it feels more like I'm just on autopilot, consuming a large amount of food because I'm feeling lonely in the evenings or worried about my health.\n\nDoctor: During these episodes of eating, do you experience a sense of guilt or self-criticism specifically about the act of eating itself, or is it more about the fear of gaining weight or health consequences?\n\nPatient: It’s really a mix of both, as I feel deeply frustrated with myself right after for losing control of my eating. But a massive driver of my anxiety is the panic about the scale creeping up and my blood pressure getting worse, which is why I end up forcing myself to throw up to get the bad stuff out before it turns into extra weight.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me more about when you started forcing yourself to throw up after eating, and how often this behavior occurs in relation to your episodes of uncontrollable eating?\n\nPatient: I started forcing myself to throw up about five months ago, right when these out-of-control eating episodes first began after my doctor's checkup. It happens about once a week, specifically on the nights when I overeat, because I feel desperate to get the bad stuff out of my system before it turns into extra weight.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate how often you engage in self-induced vomiting as a means to compensate for the calories consumed during these episodes, and does this behavior occur exclusively after the uncontrollable eating episodes or at other times as well?\n\nPatient: I make myself throw up about once a week, and it only ever happens right after those nights when I lose control and overeat. I never do it at any other time during the week. It is strictly a desperate attempt to get the food out of my system so it doesn't turn into extra weight.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever used any other methods to compensate for the calories consumed, such as excessive exercise, laxatives, or diuretics, in addition to self-induced vomiting?\n\nPatient: No, I’ve never used laxatives, water pills, or done any kind of extreme workouts. Honestly, besides making myself throw up to get the bad stuff out, the only other thing I do is try to rigidly restrict my eating the next day to make up for it.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any physical symptoms or health concerns as a result of your self-induced vomiting, such as tooth problems, throat issues, or electrolyte imbalances?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't noticed any of those specific issues like tooth or throat problems. However, I do often feel quite worn out and queasy the next morning.\n\nDoctor: Besides self-induced vomiting, do you also use other purging methods like laxatives, diuretics, or enemas to compensate for the calories consumed during these episodes?\n\nPatient: No, I have never used laxatives, diuretics, or enemas. Forcing myself to throw up is the only method I use to get the bad food out of my system.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate the average amount of weight you try to maintain or lose through these behaviors of binge eating followed by self-induced vomiting and dietary restriction?\n\nPatient: I don't really have a specific target weight or a set number of pounds I'm trying to lose. It's more about a general fear of gaining any weight at all and wanting to prevent the scale from going up. I just panic at the thought of putting on even a pound or two.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm if your self-induced vomiting and dietary restriction behaviors are primarily aimed at preventing weight gain, rather than addressing any body image concerns or a perceived need to be extremely thin?\n\nPatient: It's actually a combination of both, because while I desperately want to prevent weight gain so I don't slide into getting \"old and fat,\" I also struggle deeply with my body image. I catch myself feeling like my entire worth as a husband and professional is tied to whether my gut is hanging over my belt. I don't need to be extremely thin, but I'm terrified of looking out of shape and letting myself go.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your fear of gaining weight and your concerns about body image influence your decision to engage in binge eating followed by purging, and do you feel that these behaviors are necessary to maintain a sense of self-worth or control over your appearance?\n\nPatient: Yes, they absolutely drive the purging, because when I think about gaining even a single pound, I panic and feel like my entire worth as a husband and professional is reduced to how my gut looks in a dress shirt. Forcing myself to throw up feels like a desperate, necessary way to \"get the bad stuff out\" before it can turn into extra weight. It's the only way I feel like I can regain a little bit of control after completely losing it during the binge.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if your binge eating episodes are typically followed by purging through self-induced vomiting as a way to compensate for the consumed calories, and does this behavior occur frequently enough to be considered a regular pattern?\n\nPatient: Yes, it has definitely become a regular pattern over the last five months. On the nights when I overeat, I always end up in the bathroom forcing myself to throw up to \"get the bad stuff out\" so it doesn't turn into extra weight. This happens pretty much once a week, right after those episodes.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm if your episodes of binge eating followed by self-induced vomiting occur regularly, such as once a week, and if this pattern has been consistent over the past five months?\n\nPatient: Yes, that is exactly correct. For about the past five months, there has been at least one night every week where I have eaten an unusually large amount of food and then forced myself to throw up afterward to try to undo it. It has been a very consistent, weekly pattern for me.\n\nDoctor: Do you experience a significant amount of fear or anxiety about gaining weight, even when you're at a normal weight, which drives your need to purge after binge eating?\n\nPatient: Yes, I get an almost panicky fear that if the scale creeps up even a pound or two, it means I’m on a downhill slide to getting old and letting myself go. That intense fear of the food turning into extra weight is exactly what drives me to force myself to throw up in the bathroom after I overeat. It feels like the only way to prevent the food from sitting on me as extra weight the next day."

Forcing myself to throw up is the only method I use to get the bad food out of my system.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate the average amount of weight you try to maintain or lose through these behaviors of binge eating followed by self-induced vomiting and dietary restriction?\n\nPatient: I don't really have a specific target weight or a set number of pounds I'm trying to lose. It's more about a general fear of gaining any weight at all and wanting to prevent the scale from going up. I just panic at the thought of putting on even a pound or two.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm if your self-induced vomiting and dietary restriction behaviors are primarily aimed at preventing weight gain, rather than addressing any body image concerns or a perceived need to be extremely thin?\n\nPatient: It's actually a combination of both, because while I desperately want to prevent weight gain so I don't slide into getting \"old and fat,\" I also struggle deeply with my body image. I catch myself feeling like my entire worth as a husband and professional is tied to whether my gut is hanging over my belt. I don't need to be extremely thin, but I'm terrified of looking out of shape and letting myself go.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your fear of gaining weight and your concerns about body image influence your decision to engage in binge eating followed by purging, and do you feel that these behaviors are necessary to maintain a sense of self-worth or control over your appearance?\n\nPatient: Yes, they absolutely drive the purging, because when I think about gaining even a single pound, I panic and feel like my entire worth as a husband and professional is reduced to how my gut looks in a dress shirt. Forcing myself to throw up feels like a desperate, necessary way to \"get the bad stuff out\" before it can turn into extra weight. It's the only way I feel like I can regain a little bit of control after completely losing it during the binge.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if your binge eating episodes are typically followed by purging through self-induced vomiting as a way to compensate for the consumed calories, and does this behavior occur frequently enough to be considered a regular pattern?\n\nPatient: Yes, it has definitely become a regular pattern over the last five months. On the nights when I overeat, I always end up in the bathroom forcing myself to throw up to \"get the bad stuff out\" so it doesn't turn into extra weight. This happens pretty much once a week, right after those episodes.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm if your episodes of binge eating followed by self-induced vomiting occur regularly, such as once a week, and if this pattern has been consistent over the past five months?\n\nPatient: Yes, that is exactly correct. For about the past five months, there has been at least one night every week where I have eaten an unusually large amount of food and then forced myself to throw up afterward to try to undo it. It has been a very consistent, weekly pattern for me.\n\nDoctor: Do you experience a significant amount of fear or anxiety about gaining weight, even when you're at a normal weight, which drives your need to purge after binge eating?\n\nPatient: Yes, I get an almost panicky fear that if the scale creeps up even a pound or two, it means I’m on a downhill slide to getting old and letting myself go. That intense fear of the food turning into extra weight is exactly what drives me to force myself to throw up in the bathroom after I overeat. It feels like the only way to prevent the food from sitting on me as extra weight the next day.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm whether your self-induced vomiting occurs exclusively as a response to binge eating episodes, or if there are instances where you vomit after eating a normal or even small amount of food, to further clarify the nature of your compensatory behaviors?\n\nPatient: Yes, I only force myself to throw up on the nights when I completely overdo it and eat a massive amount of food. I never do this after eating a normal or small meal. It is strictly a desperate reaction to those specific evening episodes where I feel like I've completely lost control.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm if your self-induced vomiting occurs at least once a week for the past three months, and is this behavior intended to compensate for the calories consumed during the binge eating episodes?"

It is strictly a desperate attempt to get the food out of my system so it doesn't turn into extra weight.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever used any other methods to compensate for the calories consumed, such as excessive exercise, laxatives, or diuretics, in addition to self-induced vomiting?\n\nPatient: No, I’ve never used laxatives, water pills, or done any kind of extreme workouts. Honestly, besides making myself throw up to get the bad stuff out, the only other thing I do is try to rigidly restrict my eating the next day to make up for it.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any physical symptoms or health concerns as a result of your self-induced vomiting, such as tooth problems, throat issues, or electrolyte imbalances?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't noticed any of those specific issues like tooth or throat problems. However, I do often feel quite worn out and queasy the next morning.\n\nDoctor: Besides self-induced vomiting, do you also use other purging methods like laxatives, diuretics, or enemas to compensate for the calories consumed during these episodes?\n\nPatient: No, I have never used laxatives, diuretics, or enemas. Forcing myself to throw up is the only method I use to get the bad food out of my system.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate the average amount of weight you try to maintain or lose through these behaviors of binge eating followed by self-induced vomiting and dietary restriction?\n\nPatient: I don't really have a specific target weight or a set number of pounds I'm trying to lose. It's more about a general fear of gaining any weight at all and wanting to prevent the scale from going up. I just panic at the thought of putting on even a pound or two.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm if your self-induced vomiting and dietary restriction behaviors are primarily aimed at preventing weight gain, rather than addressing any body image concerns or a perceived need to be extremely thin?\n\nPatient: It's actually a combination of both, because while I desperately want to prevent weight gain so I don't slide into getting \"old and fat,\" I also struggle deeply with my body image. I catch myself feeling like my entire worth as a husband and professional is tied to whether my gut is hanging over my belt. I don't need to be extremely thin, but I'm terrified of looking out of shape and letting myself go.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your fear of gaining weight and your concerns about body image influence your decision to engage in binge eating followed by purging, and do you feel that these behaviors are necessary to maintain a sense of self-worth or control over your appearance?\n\nPatient: Yes, they absolutely drive the purging, because when I think about gaining even a single pound, I panic and feel like my entire worth as a husband and professional is reduced to how my gut looks in a dress shirt. Forcing myself to throw up feels like a desperate, necessary way to \"get the bad stuff out\" before it can turn into extra weight. It's the only way I feel like I can regain a little bit of control after completely losing it during the binge.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if your binge eating episodes are typically followed by purging through self-induced vomiting as a way to compensate for the consumed calories, and does this behavior occur frequently enough to be considered a regular pattern?\n\nPatient: Yes, it has definitely become a regular pattern over the last five months. On the nights when I overeat, I always end up in the bathroom forcing myself to throw up to \"get the bad stuff out\" so it doesn't turn into extra weight. This happens pretty much once a week, right after those episodes.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm if your episodes of binge eating followed by self-induced vomiting occur regularly, such as once a week, and if this pattern has been consistent over the past five months?\n\nPatient: Yes, that is exactly correct. For about the past five months, there has been at least one night every week where I have eaten an unusually large amount of food and then forced myself to throw up afterward to try to undo it. It has been a very consistent, weekly pattern for me.\n\nDoctor: Do you experience a significant amount of fear or anxiety about gaining weight, even when you're at a normal weight, which drives your need to purge after binge eating?\n\nPatient: Yes, I get an almost panicky fear that if the scale creeps up even a pound or two, it means I’m on a downhill slide to getting old and letting myself go. That intense fear of the food turning into extra weight is exactly what drives me to force myself to throw up in the bathroom after I overeat. It feels like the only way to prevent the food from sitting on me as extra weight the next day.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm whether your self-induced vomiting occurs exclusively as a response to binge eating episodes, or if there are instances where you vomit after eating a normal or even small amount of food, to further clarify the nature of your compensatory behaviors?\n\nPatient: Yes, I only force myself to throw up on the nights when I completely overdo it and eat a massive amount of food. I never do this after eating a normal or small meal. It is strictly a desperate reaction to those specific evening episodes where I feel like I've completely lost control.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm if your self-induced vomiting occurs at least once a week for the past three months, and is this behavior intended to compensate for the calories consumed during the binge eating episodes?\n\nPatient: Yes, I can confirm that it happens at least once a week, though it has actually been going on for about five months now rather than just three. It is absolutely intended to make up for all that food, as I force myself to throw up to \"get the bad stuff out\" so it doesn't turn into extra weight.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm if your self-induced vomiting has occurred at least once a week for the past three months, and is this frequency consistent with your overall pattern of binge eating followed by purging?\n\nPatient: Yes, I can absolutely confirm that. It has been happening at least once a week, and it always follows those nights when I lose control and overeat. For me, it feels more like I'm just on autopilot, consuming a large amount of food because I'm feeling lonely in the evenings or worried about my health.\n\nDoctor: During these episodes of eating, do you experience a sense of guilt or self-criticism specifically about the act of eating itself, or is it more about the fear of gaining weight or health consequences?\n\nPatient: It’s really a mix of both, as I feel deeply frustrated with myself right after for losing control of my eating. But a massive driver of my anxiety is the panic about the scale creeping up and my blood pressure getting worse, which is why I end up forcing myself to throw up to get the bad stuff out before it turns into extra weight.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me more about when you started forcing yourself to throw up after eating, and how often this behavior occurs in relation to your episodes of uncontrollable eating?\n\nPatient: I started forcing myself to throw up about five months ago, right when these out-of-control eating episodes first began after my doctor's checkup. It happens about once a week, specifically on the nights when I overeat, because I feel desperate to get the bad stuff out of my system before it turns into extra weight.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate how often you engage in self-induced vomiting as a means to compensate for the calories consumed during these episodes, and does this behavior occur exclusively after the uncontrollable eating episodes or at other times as well?\n\nPatient: I make myself throw up about once a week, and it only ever happens right after those nights when I lose control and overeat. I never do it at any other time during the week. It is strictly a desperate attempt to get the food out of my system so it doesn't turn into extra weight.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever used any other methods to compensate for the calories consumed, such as excessive exercise, laxatives, or diuretics, in addition to self-induced vomiting?\n\nPatient: No, I’ve never used laxatives, water pills, or done any kind of extreme workouts. Honestly, besides making myself throw up to get the bad stuff out, the only other thing I do is try to rigidly restrict my eating the next day to make up for it.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any physical symptoms or health concerns as a result of your self-induced vomiting, such as tooth problems, throat issues, or electrolyte imbalances?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't noticed any of those specific issues like tooth or throat problems. However, I do often feel quite worn out and queasy the next morning.\n\nDoctor: Besides self-induced vomiting, do you also use other purging methods like laxatives, diuretics, or enemas to compensate for the calories consumed during these episodes?\n\nPatient: No, I have never used laxatives, diuretics, or enemas. Forcing myself to throw up is the only method I use to get the bad food out of my system.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate the average amount of weight you try to maintain or lose through these behaviors of binge eating followed by self-induced vomiting and dietary restriction?\n\nPatient: I don't really have a specific target weight or a set number of pounds I'm trying to lose. It's more about a general fear of gaining any weight at all and wanting to prevent the scale from going up. I just panic at the thought of putting on even a pound or two.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm if your self-induced vomiting and dietary restriction behaviors are primarily aimed at preventing weight gain, rather than addressing any body image concerns or a perceived need to be extremely thin?\n\nPatient: It's actually a combination of both, because while I desperately want to prevent weight gain so I don't slide into getting \"old and fat,\" I also struggle deeply with my body image. I catch myself feeling like my entire worth as a husband and professional is tied to whether my gut is hanging over my belt. I don't need to be extremely thin, but I'm terrified of looking out of shape and letting myself go.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your fear of gaining weight and your concerns about body image influence your decision to engage in binge eating followed by purging, and do you feel that these behaviors are necessary to maintain a sense of self-worth or control over your appearance?\n\nPatient: Yes, they absolutely drive the purging, because when I think about gaining even a single pound, I panic and feel like my entire worth as a husband and professional is reduced to how my gut looks in a dress shirt. Forcing myself to throw up feels like a desperate, necessary way to \"get the bad stuff out\" before it can turn into extra weight. It's the only way I feel like I can regain a little bit of control after completely losing it during the binge.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if your binge eating episodes are typically followed by purging through self-induced vomiting as a way to compensate for the consumed calories, and does this behavior occur frequently enough to be considered a regular pattern?\n\nPatient: Yes, it has definitely become a regular pattern over the last five months. On the nights when I overeat, I always end up in the bathroom forcing myself to throw up to \"get the bad stuff out\" so it doesn't turn into extra weight. This happens pretty much once a week, right after those episodes.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm if your episodes of binge eating followed by self-induced vomiting occur regularly, such as once a week, and if this pattern has been consistent over the past five months?\n\nPatient: Yes, that is exactly correct. For about the past five months, there has been at least one night every week where I have eaten an unusually large amount of food and then forced myself to throw up afterward to try to undo it. It has been a very consistent, weekly pattern for me.\n\nDoctor: Do you experience a significant amount of fear or anxiety about gaining weight, even when you're at a normal weight, which drives your need to purge after binge eating?\n\nPatient: Yes, I get an almost panicky fear that if the scale creeps up even a pound or two, it means I’m on a downhill slide to getting old and letting myself go. That intense fear of the food turning into extra weight is exactly what drives me to force myself to throw up in the bathroom after I overeat. It feels like the only way to prevent the food from sitting on me as extra weight the next day.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm whether your self-induced vomiting occurs exclusively as a response to binge eating episodes, or if there are instances where you vomit after eating a normal or even small amount of food, to further clarify the nature of your compensatory behaviors?\n\nPatient: Yes, I only force myself to throw up on the nights when I completely overdo it and eat a massive amount of food. I never do this after eating a normal or small meal. It is strictly a desperate reaction to those specific evening episodes where I feel like I've completely lost control.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm if your self-induced vomiting occurs at least once a week for the past three months, and is this behavior intended to compensate for the calories consumed during the binge eating episodes?\n\nPatient: Yes, I can confirm that it happens at least once a week, though it has actually been going on for about five months now rather than just three. It is absolutely intended to make up for all that food, as I force myself to throw up to \"get the bad stuff out\" so it doesn't turn into extra weight.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm if your self-induced vomiting has occurred at least once a week for the past three months, and is this frequency consistent with your overall pattern of binge eating followed by purging?\n\nPatient: Yes, I can absolutely confirm that. It has been happening at least once a week, and it always follows those nights when I lose control and overeat. To be precise, this consistent pattern has actually been going on for about five months now, ever since my doctor first brought up my weight.\n\nDoctor: Do you experience any episodes of binge eating without subsequent purging, or does purging always follow your binge eating episodes?\n\nPatient: Purging almost always follows those nights when I lose control and overeat. It has become my consistent way of trying to \"undo\" the damage and manage the sheer panic I feel about gaining weight after an episode. I rarely ever have a night where I overeat like that and don't end up forcing myself to throw up.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate how many times you have engaged in self-induced vomiting as a means to compensate for binge eating episodes over the past three months, and does this occur frequently enough to be considered a regular compensatory behavior for you?"

However, I do often feel quite worn out and queasy the next morning.\n\nDoctor: Besides self-induced vomiting, do you also use other purging methods like laxatives, diuretics, or enemas to compensate for the calories consumed during these episodes?\n\nPatient: No, I have never used laxatives, diuretics, or enemas. Forcing myself to throw up is the only method I use to get the bad food out of my system.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate the average amount of weight you try to maintain or lose through these behaviors of binge eating followed by self-induced vomiting and dietary restriction?\n\nPatient: I don't really have a specific target weight or a set number of pounds I'm trying to lose. It's more about a general fear of gaining any weight at all and wanting to prevent the scale from going up. I just panic at the thought of putting on even a pound or two.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm if your self-induced vomiting and dietary restriction behaviors are primarily aimed at preventing weight gain, rather than addressing any body image concerns or a perceived need to be extremely thin?\n\nPatient: It's actually a combination of both, because while I desperately want to prevent weight gain so I don't slide into getting \"old and fat,\" I also struggle deeply with my body image. I catch myself feeling like my entire worth as a husband and professional is tied to whether my gut is hanging over my belt. I don't need to be extremely thin, but I'm terrified of looking out of shape and letting myself go.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your fear of gaining weight and your concerns about body image influence your decision to engage in binge eating followed by purging, and do you feel that these behaviors are necessary to maintain a sense of self-worth or control over your appearance?\n\nPatient: Yes, they absolutely drive the purging, because when I think about gaining even a single pound, I panic and feel like my entire worth as a husband and professional is reduced to how my gut looks in a dress shirt. Forcing myself to throw up feels like a desperate, necessary way to \"get the bad stuff out\" before it can turn into extra weight. It's the only way I feel like I can regain a little bit of control after completely losing it during the binge.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if your binge eating episodes are typically followed by purging through self-induced vomiting as a way to compensate for the consumed calories, and does this behavior occur frequently enough to be considered a regular pattern?\n\nPatient: Yes, it has definitely become a regular pattern over the last five months. On the nights when I overeat, I always end up in the bathroom forcing myself to throw up to \"get the bad stuff out\" so it doesn't turn into extra weight. This happens pretty much once a week, right after those episodes.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm if your episodes of binge eating followed by self-induced vomiting occur regularly, such as once a week, and if this pattern has been consistent over the past five months?\n\nPatient: Yes, that is exactly correct. For about the past five months, there has been at least one night every week where I have eaten an unusually large amount of food and then forced myself to throw up afterward to try to undo it. It has been a very consistent, weekly pattern for me.\n\nDoctor: Do you experience a significant amount of fear or anxiety about gaining weight, even when you're at a normal weight, which drives your need to purge after binge eating?\n\nPatient: Yes, I get an almost panicky fear that if the scale creeps up even a pound or two, it means I’m on a downhill slide to getting old and letting myself go. That intense fear of the food turning into extra weight is exactly what drives me to force myself to throw up in the bathroom after I overeat. It feels like the only way to prevent the food from sitting on me as extra weight the next day.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm whether your self-induced vomiting occurs exclusively as a response to binge eating episodes, or if there are instances where you vomit after eating a normal or even small amount of food, to further clarify the nature of your compensatory behaviors?\n\nPatient: Yes, I only force myself to throw up on the nights when I completely overdo it and eat a massive amount of food. I never do this after eating a normal or small meal. It is strictly a desperate reaction to those specific evening episodes where I feel like I've completely lost control.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm if your self-induced vomiting occurs at least once a week for the past three months, and is this behavior intended to compensate for the calories consumed during the binge eating episodes?\n\nPatient: Yes, I can confirm that it happens at least once a week, though it has actually been going on for about five months now rather than just three. It is absolutely intended to make up for all that food, as I force myself to throw up to \"get the bad stuff out\" so it doesn't turn into extra weight.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm if your self-induced vomiting has occurred at least once a week for the past three months, and is this frequency consistent with your overall pattern of binge eating followed by purging?\n\nPatient: Yes, I can absolutely confirm that. It has been happening at least once a week, and it always follows those nights when I lose control and overeat. To be precise, this consistent pattern has actually been going on for about five months now, ever since my doctor first brought up my weight.\n\nDoctor: Do you experience any episodes of binge eating without subsequent purging, or does purging always follow your binge eating episodes?\n\nPatient: Purging almost always follows those nights when I lose control and overeat. It has become my consistent way of trying to \"undo\" the damage and manage the sheer panic I feel about gaining weight after an episode. I rarely ever have a night where I overeat like that and don't end up forcing myself to throw up.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate how many times you have engaged in self-induced vomiting as a means to compensate for binge eating episodes over the past three months, and does this occur frequently enough to be considered a regular compensatory behavior for you?\n\nPatient: Yes, it has definitely become a regular pattern for me. Over the past three months, it has happened at least once a week, so that would be about 12 or 13 times in total. I do it after those evening episodes as a way to \"get the bad stuff out\" and prevent myself from gaining weight.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever considered or used any other purging methods besides self-induced vomiting, such as laxatives or diuretics, to compensate for the calories consumed during binge eating episodes, even if only occasionally?\n\nPatient: No, I have never used laxatives, diuretics, or any other purging methods to make up for the food. Forcing myself to throw up is the only thing I resort to so I can get it out of my system.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel that your self-induced vomiting is effective in preventing weight gain and maintaining your desired body image, or are there other factors that contribute to your decision to continue this behavior?"
  }

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
In my mind, I tell myself it's effective because it "gets the bad stuff out" so it doesn't sit on me as extra weight, which helps ease my intense panic about gaining even a pound or two. It feels like a desperate but necessary measure because I've started believing my whole worth as a husband and professional comes down to whether my gut is hanging over my belt. It's the only way I feel I can protect my image and keep from completely letting myself go, even if it is distressing.

Reply naturally in English as the Patient to the last Doctor utterance.\nAnswer only the question, in 2–3 sentences maximum.\n\n[Dialogue]\nDoctor: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see us today?\n\nPatient: Thank you for seeing me, doctor. To be honest, once I start eating in the evenings, it feels like I can’t stop myself, no matter how much I tell myself I should. It has really started to frighten me because I'm usually a very disciplined person.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe a typical episode where you feel like you can't stop eating, and do you experience any feelings of guilt or shame afterwards?\n\nPatient: Typically, after my wife goes to bed, I’ll start with some leftovers but end up eating half a pan of macaroni and cheese, fried chicken, and snacks like my hands are on autopilot. Afterward, I feel this deep sense of regret and shame because I just couldn't stop myself. It really frightens me how completely out of control I feel in those moments.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced similar episodes of feeling out of control, but in a sexual context, or is this loss of control primarily related to eating?\n\nPatient: No, nothing like that at all. This loss of control is strictly limited to food and eating. I manage every other part of my life very carefully and meticulously, so I've never experienced anything like this in a sexual context or any other area.\n\nDoctor: How often do these episodes of uncontrollable eating occur, and have you noticed any pattern or trigger that seems to lead up to them?\n\nPatient: These episodes have been happening about once a week for the past five months. They usually trigger in the evenings when I'm alone after my wife goes to sleep or when I'm staying up doing paperwork, especially since my doctor warned me about my blood pressure and weight.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe if there's any sexual behavior or fantasies that you feel are excessive or difficult to control, even if you mentioned it's not similar to the eating episodes, to help clarify some diagnostic possibilities?\n\nPatient: No, I don't experience anything like that. I don't have any excessive or uncontrollable sexual behaviors or fantasies, as that is just not something I struggle with. My difficulties are strictly around my eating.\n\nDoctor: Do you often eat very rapidly during these episodes or eat until you feel uncomfortably full, and have you noticed if these episodes are preceded by a feeling of tension that is relieved by eating?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure about eating particularly fast or feeling a release of tension. For me, it feels more like I'm just on autopilot, consuming a large amount of food because I'm feeling lonely in the evenings or worried about my health.\n\nDoctor: During these episodes of eating, do you experience a sense of guilt or self-criticism specifically about the act of eating itself, or is it more about the fear of gaining weight or health consequences?\n\nPatient: It’s really a mix of both, as I feel deeply frustrated with myself right after for losing control of my eating. But a massive driver of my anxiety is the panic about the scale creeping up and my blood pressure getting worse, which is why I end up forcing myself to throw up to get the bad stuff out before it turns into extra weight.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me more about when you started forcing yourself to throw up after eating, and how often this behavior occurs in relation to your episodes of uncontrollable eating?\n\nPatient: I started forcing myself to throw up about five months ago, right when these out-of-control eating episodes first began after my doctor's checkup. It happens about once a week, specifically on the nights when I overeat, because I feel desperate to get the bad stuff out of my system before it turns into extra weight.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate how often you engage in self-induced vomiting as a means to compensate for the calories consumed during these episodes, and does this behavior occur exclusively after the uncontrollable eating episodes or at other times as well?\n\nPatient: I make myself throw up about once a week, and it only ever happens right after those nights when I lose control and overeat. I never do it at any other time during the week. It is strictly a desperate attempt to get the food out of my system so it doesn't turn into extra weight.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever used any other methods to compensate for the calories consumed, such as excessive exercise, laxatives, or diuretics, in addition to self-induced vomiting?\n\nPatient: No, I’ve never used laxatives, water pills, or done any kind of extreme workouts. Honestly, besides making myself throw up to get the bad stuff out, the only other thing I do is try to rigidly restrict my eating the next day to make up for it.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any physical symptoms or health concerns as a result of your self-induced vomiting, such as tooth problems, throat issues, or electrolyte imbalances?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't noticed any of those specific issues like tooth or throat problems. However, I do often feel quite worn out and queasy the next morning.\n\nDoctor: Besides self-induced vomiting, do you also use other purging methods like laxatives, diuretics, or enemas to compensate for the calories consumed during these episodes?\n\nPatient: No, I have never used laxatives, diuretics, or enemas. Forcing myself to throw up is the only method I use to get the bad food out of my system.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate the average amount of weight you try to maintain or lose through these behaviors of binge eating followed by self-induced vomiting and dietary restriction?\n\nPatient: I don't really have a specific target weight or a set number of pounds I'm trying to lose. It's more about a general fear of gaining any weight at all and wanting to prevent the scale from going up. I just panic at the thought of putting on even a pound or two.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm if your self-induced vomiting and dietary restriction behaviors are primarily aimed at preventing weight gain, rather than addressing any body image concerns or a perceived need to be extremely thin?\n\nPatient: It's actually a combination of both, because while I desperately want to prevent weight gain so I don't slide into getting \"old and fat,\" I also struggle deeply with my body image. I catch myself feeling like my entire worth as a husband and professional is tied to whether my gut is hanging over my belt. I don't need to be extremely thin, but I'm terrified of looking out of shape and letting myself go.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your fear of gaining weight and your concerns about body image influence your decision to engage in binge eating followed by purging, and do you feel that these behaviors are necessary to maintain a sense of self-worth or control over your appearance?\n\nPatient: Yes, they absolutely drive the purging, because when I think about gaining even a single pound, I panic and feel like my entire worth as a husband and professional is reduced to how my gut looks in a dress shirt. Forcing myself to throw up feels like a desperate, necessary way to \"get the bad stuff out\" before it can turn into extra weight. It's the only way I feel like I can regain a little bit of control after completely losing it during the binge.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if your binge eating episodes are typically followed by purging through self-induced vomiting as a way to compensate for the consumed calories, and does this behavior occur frequently enough to be considered a regular pattern?\n\nPatient: Yes, it has definitely become a regular pattern over the last five months. On the nights when I overeat, I always end up in the bathroom forcing myself to throw up to \"get the bad stuff out\" so it doesn't turn into extra weight. This happens pretty much once a week, right after those episodes.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm if your episodes of binge eating followed by self-induced vomiting occur regularly, such as once a week, and if this pattern has been consistent over the past five months?\n\nPatient: Yes, that is exactly correct. For about the past five months, there has been at least one night every week where I have eaten an unusually large amount of food and then forced myself to throw up afterward to try to undo it. It has been a very consistent, weekly pattern for me.\n\nDoctor: Do you experience a significant amount of fear or anxiety about gaining weight, even when you're at a normal weight, which drives your need to purge after binge eating?\n\nPatient: Yes, I get an almost panicky fear that if the scale creeps up even a pound or two, it means I’m on a downhill slide to getting old and letting myself go. That intense fear of the food turning into extra weight is exactly what drives me to force myself to throw up in the bathroom after I overeat. It feels like the only way to prevent the food from sitting on me as extra weight the next day.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm whether your self-induced vomiting occurs exclusively as a response to binge eating episodes, or if there are instances where you vomit after eating a normal or even small amount of food, to further clarify the nature of your compensatory behaviors?\n\nPatient: Yes, I only force myself to throw up on the nights when I completely overdo it and eat a massive amount of food. I never do this after eating a normal or small meal. It is strictly a desperate reaction to those specific evening episodes where I feel like I've completely lost control.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm if your self-induced vomiting occurs at least once a week for the past three months, and is this behavior intended to compensate for the calories consumed during the binge eating episodes?\n\nPatient: Yes, I can confirm that it happens at least once a week, though it has actually been going on for about five months now rather than just three. It is absolutely intended to make up for all that food, as I force myself to throw up to \"get the bad stuff out\" so it doesn't turn into extra weight.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm if your self-induced vomiting has occurred at least once a week for the past three months, and is this frequency consistent with your overall pattern of binge eating followed by purging?\n\nPatient: Yes, I can absolutely confirm that. It has been happening at least once a week, and it always follows those nights when I lose control and overeat. To be precise, this consistent pattern has actually been going on for about five months now, ever since my doctor first brought up my weight.\n\nDoctor: Do you experience any episodes of binge eating without subsequent purging, or does purging always follow your binge eating episodes?\n\nPatient: Purging almost always follows those nights when I lose control and overeat. Forcing myself to throw up is the only thing I resort to so I can get it out of my system.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel that your self-induced vomiting is effective in preventing weight gain and maintaining your desired body image, or are there other factors that contribute to your decision to continue this behavior?\n\nPatient: In my mind, I tell myself it's effective because it \"gets the bad stuff out\" so it doesn't sit on me as extra weight, which helps ease my intense panic about gaining even a pound or two. It is strictly a desperate attempt to get the food out of my system so it doesn't turn into extra weight.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever used any other methods to compensate for the calories consumed, such as excessive exercise, laxatives, or diuretics, in addition to self-induced vomiting?\n\nPatient: No, I’ve never used laxatives, water pills, or done any kind of extreme workouts. Honestly, besides making myself throw up to get the bad stuff out, the only other thing I do is try to rigidly restrict my eating the next day to make up for it.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any physical symptoms or health concerns as a result of your self-induced vomiting, such as tooth problems, throat issues, or electrolyte imbalances?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't noticed any of those specific issues like tooth or throat problems. However, I do often feel quite worn out and queasy the next morning.\n\nDoctor: Besides self-induced vomiting, do you also use other purging methods like laxatives, diuretics, or enemas to compensate for the calories consumed during these episodes?\n\nPatient: No, I have never used laxatives, diuretics, or enemas. Forcing myself to throw up is the only method I use to get the bad food out of my system.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate the average amount of weight you try to maintain or lose through these behaviors of binge eating followed by self-induced vomiting and dietary restriction?\n\nPatient: I don't really have a specific target weight or a set number of pounds I'm trying to lose. It's more about a general fear of gaining any weight at all and wanting to prevent the scale from going up. I just panic at the thought of putting on even a pound or two.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm if your self-induced vomiting and dietary restriction behaviors are primarily aimed at preventing weight gain, rather than addressing any body image concerns or a perceived need to be extremely thin?\n\nPatient: It's actually a combination of both, because while I desperately want to prevent weight gain so I don't slide into getting \"old and fat,\" I also struggle deeply with my body image. I catch myself feeling like my entire worth as a husband and professional is tied to whether my gut is hanging over my belt. I don't need to be extremely thin, but I'm terrified of looking out of shape and letting myself go.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your fear of gaining weight and your concerns about body image influence your decision to engage in binge eating followed by purging, and do you feel that these behaviors are necessary to maintain a sense of self-worth or control over your appearance?\n\nPatient: Yes, they absolutely drive the purging, because when I think about gaining even a single pound, I panic and feel like my entire worth as a husband and professional is reduced to how my gut looks in a dress shirt. Forcing myself to throw up feels like a desperate, necessary way to \"get the bad stuff out\" before it can turn into extra weight. That intense fear of the food turning into extra weight is exactly what drives me to force myself to throw up in the bathroom after I overeat. It feels like the only way to prevent the food from sitting on me as extra weight the next day.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm whether your self-induced vomiting occurs exclusively as a response to binge eating episodes, or if there are instances where you vomit after eating a normal or even small amount of food, to further clarify the nature of your compensatory behaviors?\n\nPatient: Yes, I only force myself to throw up on the nights when I completely overdo it and eat a massive amount of food. I never do this after eating a normal or small meal. It is strictly a desperate reaction to those specific evening episodes where I feel like I've completely lost control.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm if your self-induced vomiting occurs at least once a week for the past three months, and is this behavior intended to compensate for the calories consumed during the binge eating episodes?\n\nPatient: Yes, I can confirm that it happens at least once a week, though it has actually been going on for about five months now rather than just three. It is absolutely intended to make up for all that food, as I force myself to throw up to \"get the bad stuff out\" so it doesn't turn into extra weight.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm if your self-induced vomiting has occurred at least once a week for the past three months, and is this frequency consistent with your overall pattern of binge eating followed by purging?\n\nPatient: Yes, I can absolutely confirm that. It has been happening at least once a week, and it always follows those nights when I lose control and overeat. To be precise, this consistent pattern has actually been going on for about five months now, ever since my doctor first brought up my weight.\n\nDoctor: Do you experience any episodes of binge eating without subsequent purging, or does purging always follow your binge eating episodes?\n\nPatient: Purging almost always follows those nights when I lose control and overeat. It has become my consistent way of trying to \"undo\" the damage and manage the sheer panic I feel about gaining weight after an episode. I rarely ever have a night where I overeat like that and don't end up forcing myself to throw up.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate how many times you have engaged in self-induced vomiting as a means to compensate for binge eating episodes over the past three months, and does this occur frequently enough to be considered a regular compensatory behavior for you?\n\nPatient: Yes, it has definitely become a regular pattern for me. Over the past three months, it has happened at least once a week, so that would be about 12 or 13 times in total. I do it after those evening episodes as a way to \"get the bad stuff out\" and prevent myself from gaining weight.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever considered or used any other purging methods besides self-induced vomiting, such as laxatives or diuretics, to compensate for the calories consumed during binge eating episodes, even if only occasionally?\n\nPatient: No, I have never used laxatives, diuretics, or any other purging methods to make up for the food. Forcing myself to throw up is the only thing I resort to so I can get it out of my system.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel that your self-induced vomiting is effective in preventing weight gain and maintaining your desired body image, or are there other factors that contribute to your decision to continue this behavior?\n\nPatient: In my mind, I tell myself it's effective because it \"gets the bad stuff out\" so it doesn't sit on me as extra weight, which helps ease my intense panic about gaining even a pound or two.
